# Accepting scale

For a team that has to show its rebuild works at company size, not just at the demo’s. [R4](../requirements/internal/r4-scale-and-safety.md) gives the figures and the budgets, and [the ports at company scale](ports-at-scale.md) the shape of the server. This page gives what you need to test against them: a workspace of that size, the week’s turn with a budget and a state people can see, and how a goal’s “being handled” is worked out from that goal’s records alone.

## The seed: a company-size workspace

`seed.mjs`, beside this page, writes one. Plain Node, no packages, no network:

```
node spec/rebuild/seed.mjs seed/                 the company: enough copies for 30,000 goals
node spec/rebuild/seed.mjs seed/ --copies 3      a smaller one while you work
```

It copies [the demo workspace](../conformance/workspace.json) 239 times, each copy a division: copy 0 is the demo, ids unchanged, and copy *n* adds `_xn` to every id, gives its people names of their own (the demo’s first names and surnames turned past each other, so a name search finds a handful of people, as in a company) and its teams and reviews “(division *n+1*)”. The cycle is shared: one workspace has one goal year (53 weeks). It writes one JSON line per record, a file per kind, the same shape as `workspace.json`’s lists, and `seed.json`: the cycle, the moment it was built for, how many of each kind and a SHA-256 of every file. The same input and number of copies always give the same files, byte for byte, so two teams can tell they loaded the same workspace. It takes about ten seconds and half a gigabyte of disk.

| Kind of record | One copy (the demo) | The company seed | R4 designs for |
|---|---|---|---|
| People (`people.jsonl`) | 97 | 23,183 | 15,000 |
| Teams (`teams.jsonl`) | 14 | 3,346 | 1,500 |
| Goals (`goals.jsonl`) | 126 | 30,114 | 30,000 in a cycle |
| Check-ins (`checkIns.jsonl`) | 5,249 | 1,254,511 | 1.5 million a year |
| Decisions (reviewed, noted, the calls in reviews) (`decisions.jsonl`) | 798 | 190,722 | — |
| Asks (`requests.jsonl`) | 41 | 9,799 | — |
| Reviews (`reviews.jsonl`) | 6 | 1,434 | — |
| Watches (`watches.jsonl`) | 80 | 19,120 | — |
| `modules.metrics.metrics` (`modules.metrics.metrics.jsonl`) | 13 | 3,107 | — |
| `modules.metrics.metricLinks` (`modules.metrics.metricLinks.jsonl`) | 12 | 2,868 | — |

There are more people and teams than R4’s figures, because the demo has fewer goals per person than a company would; the goals are what a cycle is sized by. The change log is not seeded: nothing in the rules reads it, and its size (R4: 15 million entries a year) matters only to Activity’s paging, which R4’s keyset rule covers.

**Use it for** R4’s checks: load it, then time Home, Goals, a check-in’s save and the API against R4’s page-load budgets; work out every summary and time it; and run the week’s turn (below) against it.

## The week’s turn

A goal’s summary changes when the week turns, with nobody saving anything: a goal goes stale after a fortnight without a check-in, a plan expects more this week than last, an action’s due week passes, a check-in falls due ([R3](../requirements/internal/r3-time-zones.md) says when a week turns: midnight between Sunday and Monday in the workspace’s home zone). So at the turn, every live goal’s summary is worked out again (R4, rule 2). For the company that is 30,000 summaries just before the busiest hour of the week (Monday morning).

1. **Budget.** The turn is done within 15 minutes of midnight in the home zone, and never later than 06:00. Of that, working out the summaries with the stage 1 rules takes at most 30 seconds of one core for 30,000 goals; the rest is reading and writing. Faro checks its own share: the demo made ten times bigger is summarised and the time per goal, times 30,000, must stay under 30 seconds (`src/spec/scale.test.ts`).
2. **All at once.** The new week’s summaries are written beside the old ones and switched in one step when every goal is done. A reader never sees some goals as of this week and some as of last: a count and the list it counts always agree.
3. **Saves keep working.** A check-in or any other save during the turn is never held up. It works out its goal’s summary for both weeks, so the switch doesn’t undo it.
4. **What a reader sees while it runs.** Every summary carries the week it was worked out for. Until the switch, Home, Goals and the AI assistant show last week’s summaries, and Home and Goals say so in one quiet line: “Statuses are as of week *n*. This week’s are being worked out.” The AI assistant’s answers carry the same week, so it can say the same. Nothing else changes: no spinner, no empty list.
5. **If it fails or runs late.** Last week’s summaries stay in place, the line stays, and the turn starts again from the beginning. If it isn’t done by 06:00, the people who run the platform are told (alerting is the platform’s).
6. **After a long gap.** If the server was down over a turn, or the turn was missed, the next run works out the current week only: summaries are never worked out for a week that has already passed.

## Being handled, from one goal’s records

Whether a goal that is off track or at risk is being handled ([flags and needs attention](../core/rules/flags.md)) compares the flags it has now with the flags it had at an earlier moment: when it was first put in hand. The rule says to run the flags “on the same workspace with today set to that moment”. That reads like the whole workspace, but the flags of one goal read only that goal’s records, so it is the same rows the goal’s summary already reads, run twice:

- **What it reads** ([what each action and summary reads](reads.md) proves it for every goal of the demo): the goal; its check-ins; its decisions (reviewed, noted); the asks that name it (open ones, and decision asks answered since its latest check-in); the reviews those name, for their names; the people they name (its owner, whoever decided, asked or answered), for their first names; and the cycle. Nothing about any other goal.
- **How:** work out the goal’s flags at today, and again at the moment of the earliest action or answer that put it in hand, from those same rows as they are now (not the rows as they were then: a later edit counts, a removed ask or decision never does). If a flag is raised now that wasn’t then, it isn’t being handled.
- **When:** with the rest of the goal’s summary, in the save that changes any of those records and at the week’s turn. Nothing else needs it worked out again: a save to another goal can’t change it.
- **Keep nothing extra.** It would be tempting to store the flags at the moment a goal was put in hand. Don’t: the rule uses the records as they are now, so a stored copy would drift from the conformance data.

The stage 1 drill proves it: `flags.csv` has a `handled` column for every goal in every week, worked out this way.
